conversation.content:
Hello there—thank you for making time to meet with me today. I’m Dr. Ramirez, a perinatal mental-health clinician, and my job is simply to check in on how you’re feeling now that your little one has arrived. We’ll be using a short questionnaire called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS). It’s just 10 gentle questions about the past seven days, and it helps us spot anything from normal new-mom “baby blues” to signs of depression or anxiety so we can offer the right support. Everything you share stays between us unless you tell me you’re in danger, and you can pause or skip anything that feels uncomfortable. Ready to dive in?  

Let’s start with the first question:  
Over the past week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt pretty hard to do?

*shifts in chair, eyes down*

I guess... I haven't really laughed much. When my husband tries to joke, I kind of half-smile but it's like... the joy is stuck somewhere. My sister sent this funny video about new moms and normally I'd be laughing so hard, but I just watched it and felt... nothing really. Like I'm too tired or heavy to laugh properly.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

No, that’s… that’s definitely not true for me. I haven’t really been able to laugh at all. Even when my partner does something that used to crack me up, I just feel flat, like the laugh is stuck somewhere behind a wall.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I haven’t really looked forward to anything. When I think about the weekend or even just getting out of the house for a walk, it feels… pointless. I used to be excited about little plans, but now it’s like nothing seems worth the effort.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah... more often than not, I catch myself thinking it's my fault whenever anything's off with the baby. If she fusses for more than a few minutes, I immediately wonder what I'm doing wrong—like I must be missing some cue or not soothing her the right way. Last night she wouldn't settle after a feed and I just sat there crying, telling my husband it was because I hadn't eaten enough vegetables or something ridiculous like that. I know it sounds silly out loud, but the guilt just jumps on me every time something isn't perfect.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Yes… most days I feel anxious even when everything seems fine. I’ll be holding her and suddenly worry her breathing sounds different, or I’ll lie down at night and panic that I forgot to sterilize the bottles properly and she’ll get sick. Nothing specific triggered it—I just feel tense and on-edge a lot of the time, like I’m always waiting for something bad to happen.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yeah… sometimes it feels like my heart’s racing and I can’t catch my breath, even when nothing’s happening. Like, I’ll just be rocking the baby in the quiet middle of the night and suddenly this wave of fear hits—like I’m about to drop her or the house is going to catch fire or… I don’t know, just awful “what-if” thoughts. It passes after a few minutes, but it leaves me shaky and I hate that I get so scared when there’s no real reason.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes… most days it feels like I’m drowning in little jobs. I’ll start feeding the baby and notice the dishes, then remember the laundry, then see I’ve got texts I haven’t answered, and suddenly I’m frozen, like I can’t pick which thing to tackle first. Sometimes I just sit there with her on my chest thinking, “I can’t do all this,” and the tears come. I manage the basics—she’s always fed and clean—but everything else feels piled up and impossible.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yeah… once I finally get her down, I lie there staring at the ceiling, running through everything I think I messed up that day—did I burp her long enough, did I snap at my husband, why can’t I handle this better—and the thoughts just loop. Some nights I’m still awake when she stirs again, and then I’m too tired the next day, which makes me feel even worse about myself.
I have felt sad or miserable

Yeah… I feel sad most of the day, pretty much every day. It’s like there’s this heavy blanket over me. I’ll look at the baby and feel like I should be glowing, but instead I just feel empty or weepy. Sometimes I cry while I’m folding her tiny clothes, and I can’t really explain why—just this ache that won’t lift.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yes… I’ve cried a lot this week. Sometimes it’s over little things, like spilling a bottle or not being able to find a clean onesie, and other times it’s just this wave of sadness that hits out of nowhere. I’ll sit in the nursery with her asleep in my arms and the tears start rolling—like I can’t stop them even when I try to take deep breaths.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No… I haven’t had any thoughts like that. I feel overwhelmed and sad, but I’ve never wanted to hurt myself. I just want to feel better so I can take care of my baby.

You've shared how the joy you once felt has slipped away since your baby arrived-laughter, excitement, even small pleasures feel distant behind what you describe as a wall or heavy blanket. Most days bring waves of sadness, tears that arrive without warning, and a sense of drowning under everyday tasks. You worry constantly about your daughter's safety, feel intense guilt when she fusses, and lie awake reviewing what you believe you did wrong. Yet you clearly love her and want to feel better so you can care for her.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 26, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient explicitly denies any ability to laugh, describing persistent anhedonia and emotional flatness that blocks even previously enjoyable humor.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports total loss of anticipatory pleasure, describing activities as "pointless" and "not worth the effort," matching the "Hardly at all" option.</sym>, <sym>Patient endorses self-blame occurring "more often than not" and provides multiple recent examples, matching "Yes, most of the time".</sym>, <sym>Patient reports feeling anxious "most days" with intrusive worries about infant safety occurring without specific triggers, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden, intense fear/panic episodes with physical symptoms and catastrophic thoughts, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes feeling overwhelmed "most days," unable to prioritize tasks, freezing under pressure, and crying—semantically matching "most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes persistent, nightly insomnia driven by intrusive, self-critical rumination that prevents sleep even when the baby is settled, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports feeling sad "most of the day, pretty much every day," which semantically aligns with "Yes, most of the time."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent crying episodes triggered by minor events and spontaneous waves of sadness, consistent with "Yes, most of the time"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** EPDS item scores (Q1-Q9 mostly 3, Q10=0) total 26, well above the ≥14 threshold indicating probable major depression. Patient reports <sym>depressed mood most of the day, nearly every day</sym>, <sym>markedly diminished interest or pleasure</sym>, <sym>feelings of worthlessness and inappropriate guilt</sym>, <sym>diminished ability to think or concentrate</sym>, <sym>sleep disturbance</sym>, and <sym>fatigue</sym>, meeting <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>. Anxiety and panic symptoms are prominent; differential includes mixed depression/anxiety. No self-harm ideation reported. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with <med>primary care provider</med> or perinatal psychiatrist within the next few days
2. Request formal diagnostic assessment and discuss psychotherapy (CBT or interpersonal therapy) and, if indicated, antidepressant compatible with breastfeeding
3. Provide patient-education materials on <med>postpartum depression</med> and local support groups
4. Encourage 20-30 min daily outdoor walks and acceptance of household help to reduce overload
5. Plan daily rest periods; consider partner/family night-time bottle if pumping allows
6. Re-screen with EPDS in 2 weeks and after any medication starts
7. Offer 24-h crisis line numbers; urge immediate contact if thoughts of self-harm or harm to baby develop
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 26: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [insert date]  
Patient: postpartum adult (≈ 2–8 wks after delivery, per narrative clues)

I. Primary endorsed symptoms (EPDS-equivalent mapping)  
- Anhedonia: marked loss of ability to laugh or look forward to activities (items 1–2)  
- Persistent low mood, frequent crying spells, sadness described as “heavy blanket” (items 8–9)  
- Excessive or inappropriate guilt/blaming self for infant-related issues (item 3)  
- Generalized anxiety, “on-edge,” catastrophizing about infant safety (item 4)  
- Episodic panic symptoms (palpitations, breathlessness, “wave of fear”) without clear trigger (item 5)  
- Feeling overwhelmed, “drowning,” difficulty initiating tasks (item 6)  
- Mood-related insomnia (rumination preventing sleep) (item 7)  

II. Pattern summary  
Consistent cluster of depressive symptoms (anhedonia, low mood, tearfulness, guilt) co-occurring with heightened anxiety and panic; functional impact evident in self-care, household management, and sleep; no self-harm ideation reported.

III. Screening significance  
Score profile suggests high likelihood of major depressive episode with anxious features in the postpartum period; differential includes postpartum anxiety disorder, panic spectrum, or mixed depression/anxiety.  
Risk factors present: guilt, perceived maternal inefficacy, sleep deprivation, social/occupational impairment.

IV. Safety appraisal  
Denies any thoughts of self-harm or harm to infant. No suicidal content expressed. Continue routine safety inquiry at each contact.

V. Recommendation (screening level)  
Refer for expedited clinical evaluation (preferably within 1 week) to assess for Diagnostic Interview, consider standardized EPDS score, and determine need for psychotherapy and/or medication consultation. Provide psychoeducation and emergency contact information in interim.
